alignment.note: Greek employs the article ὁ with postpositive δέ; Syriac and Latin lack the article (Syriac ܦܝܠܛܘܣ ܕܝܢ, Latin Pilatus autem), reflecting their respective grammatical norms for proper nouns and adversative conjunctions.

Greek uses the participial phrase βουλόμενος τῷ ὄχλῳ τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι ('desiring to do what was satisfactory to the crowd'), employing the adjective ἱκανόν with articular construction. Latin renders this idiomatically as volens populo satisfacere ('wishing to satisfy the people'), using the verb satisfacere. Syriac restructures entirely with ܨܒܐ ܕܢܥܒܕ ܨܒܝܢܐ ܠܟܢܫܐ ('he desired to do the will/desire of the crowd'), employing the cognate noun ܨܒܝܢܐ ('will, desire') rather than an adjectival or verbal equivalent of 'satisfactory.'

Greek uses the aorist participle φραγελλώσας ('having flogged') in attributive position modifying the main verb παρέδωκεν, creating a temporal sequence. Latin employs the ablative absolute construction flagellis cæsum ('having been beaten with whips'), a perfect passive participle with instrumental ablative. Syriac restructures with the temporal particle ܟܕ ܡܢܓܕ ('while/when scourged'), using a different syntactic frame but preserving the temporal relationship between scourging and handing over.

Greek employs ἵνα with aorist passive subjunctive σταυρωθῇ to express purpose ('that he might be crucified'). Latin mirrors this with ut + subjunctive crucifigeretur. Syriac uses the prefixed ܕ- on the imperfect ܕܢܙܕܩܦ, a standard Syriac purpose construction functionally equivalent to the Greek and Latin, though morphologically distinct.
